title: Canadian blanket: Unhealthy haze from wildfires in Canada settles over state
summary: Health officials were warning Marylanders to avoid excessive activity and stay inside if possible, with Code Red and more severe Code Purple conditions spreading across the state as smoke from Canadian wildfires settled over the region.
content:
By Tadiwos Abedje

Health officials were warning Marylanders to avoid excessive activity and stay inside if possible, with Code Red and more severe Code Purple conditions spreading across the state as smoke from Canadian wildfires settled over the region.

The smoke is being carried into the region by prevailing winds and comes as temperatures are expected to reach into the 90s today and tomorrow. Code Red conditions are unhealthy and Code Purple are very unhealthy.

Walking outside Friday morning, residents were met with blurry skies that reeked of smoke.

The thick smoke in the sky Friday is similar to what happened during the summer of 2023 when the region was under code red, purple and maroon alerts, according to 7News First Alert Meteorologist Eileen Whelan.

“The darker the color means a higher concentration of smoke particles in the air, so that can make it more difficult to breathe, especially if you’re doing strenuous activity outdoors, taking deeper breaths,” Whelan said.

Gov. Wes Moore urged Marylanders to take “extra precaution” as they moved about Friday and Saturday.

“At-risk populations should stay indoors and keep your windows closed to keep yourself safe,” he said in a prepared statement. “Please make sure to check in on your family, neighbors and loved ones.”

With Code Purple air quality, taking a deep breath outdoors is “very unhealthy” for everyone, especially people with certain health conditions, according to the Metropolitan Washington Council of Governments.

“Just walking around outside, I could feel a little bit of tightness and burning in my chest,” said Dr. Bobby Mahajan, chief of interventional pulmonology with Inova Health System.

Smoke from wildfires contains fine particulates that are so small they bypass the nose and throat’s natural filters, and travel into the lungs. Once in the lungs, the smoky air can cause irritation, inflammation and narrowing of the airways.

The region’s typical summer combination of heat and humidity is taken to the next level with the addition of the wildfire smoke.

“That’s not only a strain on your muscles and your body with the temperature, but you’re actually affecting your lungs themselves, because every breath you’re taking you’re taking in noxious particulate matter,” Mahajan said.

For someone with lung disease, their airways may already be narrowed or inflamed. Extra inflammation from smoke or pollution could constrict airways ever more, according to Mahajan.

Meteorologists expect conditions will start to improve over the weekend.

“As we move through the evening and into the overnight, our winds will change direction, and that’s going to improve our air quality,” said 7News First Alert Meteorologist Steve Rudin. “They’ll be from the south as we head through the overnight, with temperatures dropping into the 70s.”

The situation could be helped by an isolated shower or thunderstorm that could pop up overnight.

An incoming cold front will start to remove the smoky air Saturday while bringing the potential of severe storms and heavy rain. It will still be hot with temperatures in the upper 80s to lower 90s.

“We’re tracking strong to severe thunderstorms, several waves of storms from late morning through the afternoon and then into the evening,” Rudin said. “Any storm that does develop will have the potential to become strong to severe with gusty winds, heavy downpours, frequent lightning, even an isolated tornado.”

Conditions will continue to improve Sunday, despite starting off muggy, with partly cloudy skies with seasonable temperatures in the upper 80s to around 90 degrees and a chance for an isolated shower.

Safety precautions

Health officials said that if people are feeling unwell or dizzy, they should all their doctor. People are encouraged to stay indoors as much as possible.

Even while inside, some people might be affected by the air.

“If you’re having symptoms of headache, itchy, watery eyes, sore throat, coughing, chest pain, chest tightness — these are all symptoms that you’re being affected by the poor air quality,” allergist and immunologist Dr. Purvi Parikh said.

Parikh said air purifiers can help filter out the dangerous particles.

The Metropolitan Washington Council of Governments has recommended that residents avoid arduous activities, take breaks where there’s clean air, wear an N95 mask and use a portable air cleaner in rooms.

The Maryland Department of Health is advising Marylanders to follow the Air Quality Action Guide, which includes information on preventing adverse effects of polluted air. For a red or purple alert, everyone should limit strenuous outdoor activity when the air is unhealthy to breathe.

Officials are also reminding people to keep an eye out for neighbors and relatives with chronic health problems who might be affected.

Current air quality information is always available at mde.maryland.gov.
author: WTOP News
